title: Backup before migrate: the ordering, the receipt, and a restore that has actually been restored
description:
SPIDR child of task-78eedd8ebc2b43c581ac21ea28648a9a (architect-fa3a3e17, 2026-09-05), which measured far over the 10-file cap: it wanted a migration engine, a published command kind with full roster backfill, a real-PostgreSQL restore proof, three UI surfaces, a Playwright journey, a live drive and docs. This row is the ENGINE and the SAFETY PROPERTY. dependsOn child 1 (task-463f195efd2f4fd2886790029a474194, the migration tool) and child 2 (task-ff41c5c9efa34494b7b91e6f0ddcb7c2, the disposable-PostgreSQL lifecycle this reuses for the restore proof).

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: applying pending migrations AFTER a `pg_dump` backup; the `moe-migration-receipt/1` record; the MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED and MIGRATION_FAILED refusals; and the restore round trip. NO command kind (that is the sibling publish row), NO UI, NO Playwright, NO live drive - all the parent's.

BACKUP BEFORE MIGRATE IS THE ORDER, and it is the only thing standing between a bad migration and lost production data. MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED must mean NOTHING IS APPLIED - a migration that ran after a failed backup is the exact scenario the receipt exists to make impossible. Assert the schema is UNTOUCHED on that path, not merely that a refusal was returned.

A BACKUP NOBODY HAS RESTORED IS A FILE, NOT A SAFETY NET. That is why the restore round trip is in this row rather than deferred: the row that writes the backup is the row that must prove it can be read back.

MEASURED AT HEAD (branch moe/work-2026-09-04) by architect-fa3a3e17:
- `git grep -c "migrate_down|MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED|moe-migration-receipt" -- apps packages` returns NOTHING. No migration surface exists at all; the gap is real in every direction.
- THE BACKUP LOCATION IS AN EXISTING CONVENTION BUT IT IS NOT EXPORTED: apps/daemon/src/bootstrap/activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33 declares `const BACKUP_DIRECTORY = ".moe-next"` and `const BACKUP_LEAF = "backups"` as MODULE-PRIVATE constants. Reusing them means exporting them (preferred - one definition) or, if that ripples, deriving the path from the same two literals with a comment naming that file as the source. Do NOT invent a second location: a second backup location is a second place to look during an incident.
- THE RECEIPT SHAPE to mirror is apps/daemon/src/repository/publish-receipt-contracts.ts (`PUBLISH_RECEIPT_VERSION` :16, `PublishRefusal` :36, `PublishReceiptV1` :41), whose null-pairing discipline - exactly one of the success member and the refusal member populated - is what makes a REFUSED receipt unambiguous.
- `internal.*` receipt kinds are OUTSIDE PAYLOAD_KEYS, the registry and the MCP roster entirely (`grep -n "internal\." apps/daemon/src/daemon-command-vocabulary.ts` = 0), so `moe-migration-receipt/1` costs NO roster backfill.

COMPOSE WITH THE DEPLOY ROW, DO NOT DUPLICATE IT: task-5d30948435524c6fa2789e1c033aafe7 owns the deploy path and is a SIBLING feature row, so no dependsOn is allowed. If the deploy path has not landed, ship this machinery behind its own entry point and say so plainly in the record.
definitionOfDone: BACKUP-BEFORE-MIGRATE ORDERING asserted offline through injectable docker/pg ports: the `pg_dump` COMPLETES before the first migration runs, proven through the ports' recorded call ORDER rather than by inspection. Mutate the service to migrate-then-backup and confirm the arm goes RED - an ordering property that has never been seen red is not evidence.

MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED MEANS ZERO MIGRATIONS APPLIED, and the assertion reads the SCHEMA, not the return value: on that path the schema is byte-for-byte untouched. This is the row's central safety property and the one whose failure loses data that cannot be recovered. Assert code AND layer.

`moe-migration-receipt/1` records {environment, sha, applied[], backupRef, APPLIED|REFUSED(code)}, mirroring apps/daemon/src/repository/publish-receipt-contracts.ts including its null-pairing (exactly one of the success member and the refusal member populated). Read it back from a REAL store and assert every member. The backupRef carries the backup's sha256 and the file exists at `<project>/.moe-next/backups/<env>/<ts>.sql`.

THE BACKUP PATH REUSES THE EXISTING CONVENTION at apps/daemon/src/bootstrap/activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33 (`.moe-next` + `backups`), which is currently module-private - either export those constants or derive from the same literals with a comment naming that file. Assert the resulting path with a grep in the completion record. A second backup location is a rejection.

THE RESTORE ROUND TRIP IS PROVEN against a REAL disposable PostgreSQL from child 2's lifecycle: back up a known schema, change it, restore, and assert the schema matches the original. A backup that has never been restored in a test is a file, not a safety net.

MIGRATION_FAILED asserts code AND layer and NAMES THE FAILING MIGRATION FILE - a generic failure is undiagnosable from a receipt. On that path the receipt is REFUSED with the failing migration named and the backup still recorded.

EVERY disposable database, container, temp directory and child process is torn down on EVERY exit path including the throwing one (epic rail 4) - teardown in a `finally`, not after the assertions. Invoke `pg_dump`/`psql`/`docker` as bare executables under shell:false with argv arrays; never a hard-coded `.cmd`, never a shell string, never a chain.

Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`. Root `pnpm test` covers no apps/** file, so say that rather than quoting a bare root count line.
taskRails: BACKUP BEFORE MIGRATE, ALWAYS. A failed backup means nothing is applied. This is the row's reason for existing and the one property whose failure loses data that cannot be recovered.
RESTORE MUST BE PROVEN, not assumed. The row that writes the backup is the row that proves it can be read back.
REUSE `.moe-next/backups` (activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33). A second backup location is a second place to look during an incident.

NO COMMAND KIND. `deployment.migrate_down` and its roster backfill belong to the sibling publish row; no edit to daemon-command-vocabulary.ts, daemon-command-registry.ts, mcp-tool-allowlist.ts, agent-spawn-contract.ts or packages/contracts.
NO UI, NO PLAYWRIGHT, NO LIVE DRIVE, NO DOCS - all belong to the parent task-78eedd8ebc2b43c581ac21ea28648a9a.
COMPOSE WITH THE DEPLOY ROW (task-5d309484), do not duplicate it. It is a SIBLING feature row so no dependsOn is allowed; if it has not landed, ship behind this row's own entry point and say so.

implementationPlan.description:
MEASURE AT CLAIM. This row sits TWO levels behind an unlanded leaf: task-463f195e (the migration tool, PLANNING at plan time) -> task-ff41c5c9 (the disposable-PostgreSQL lifecycle, PLANNING, held by architect-b63fabf3) -> this row. Both are in your dependsOn, so the runtime withholds the WORKING claim until they land — but re-measure rather than assume.

Confirm the gap is still real (it was, at plan time): `git grep -c "migrate_down\|MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED\|moe-migration-receipt" -- apps packages` returns NOTHING. No migration surface exists in any direction, so nothing here is a duplicate.

Read from get_context.epicSiblings rather than re-deriving: child 1's completionSummary for the migration tool's actual invocation, and child 2's for the disposable-PostgreSQL lifecycle's entry point and container naming — DoD 5's restore round trip REUSES that lifecycle rather than standing up a second one. If child 2 shipped its container lifecycle behind a flag-gated real-docker lane (which is how its sibling deploy row does it), your DoD 5 arm inherits that gate; find out now, not at step 6.

COMPOSE WITH THE DEPLOY ROW, DO NOT DUPLICATE IT (rail 6). task-5d309484 owns the deploy path and is a SIBLING feature row, so no dependsOn is allowed. Measure whether it has landed. If it has not, ship this machinery behind THIS row's own entry point and say so plainly in the completion record — do not wire into a deploy path that does not exist, and do not build a second one.

THE BACKUP PATH — REUSE THE CONVENTION, DO NOT MINT A THIRD TRANSCRIPTION. Measured at HEAD: `apps/daemon/src/bootstrap/activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33` declares `const BACKUP_DIRECTORY = ".moe-next"` and `const BACKUP_LEAF = "backups"` as MODULE-PRIVATE constants, joined at :154 as `join(input.projectRoot, BACKUP_DIRECTORY, BACKUP_LEAF)`.

AND THEY ARE ALREADY TRANSCRIBED ONCE MORE: `apps/daemon/src/daemon-main-activation-boot.test.ts:35-36` re-declares both literals locally and joins them at :156. So there are already TWO copies, and inventing a third is exactly what rail 3 forbids — a second backup location is a second place to look during an incident, and a third transcription is a third place for them to drift.

PREFER EXPORTING the two constants from activation-receipts-measure.ts and importing them here: one definition, and the ripple is small because only that module consumes them in production. If exporting ripples further than you measure, derive the path from the same two literals with a comment NAMING activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33 as the source of truth.

DO NOT also refactor `daemon-main-activation-boot.test.ts` to import them. It is out of this row's scope, it is a file you do not own, and tidying it would put an unrelated test in your diff. Note it in the step note as a follow-up observation instead.

Assert the resulting path with a grep in the completion record (DoD 4): the backup file lands at `<project>/.moe-next/backups/<env>/<ts>.sql`.

THE RECEIPT CONTRACTS — a new focused module plus its one-line `.js` bridge, mirroring `apps/daemon/src/repository/publish-receipt-contracts.ts`.

Copy its NULL-PAIRING DISCIPLINE, which is the thing that makes a REFUSED receipt unambiguous. Measured shape: `PublishReceiptV1` (:41-53) carries `outcome: "PUSHED" | "REFUSED"` alongside `refusal: PublishRefusal | null` and nullable success members (`sha`, `branch`, `url`), with `PublishRefusal` (:36-39) being `{ code, detail }`. Exactly one side is populated.

Yours: `moe-migration-receipt/1` recording `{ environment, sha, applied[], backupRef, outcome: "APPLIED" | "REFUSED", refusal: { code, detail } | null }`. Mirror the version constant (`PUBLISH_RECEIPT_VERSION` :16) and the decode-result union (`PublishReceiptDecodeResult` :55-57) so a malformed receipt answers a typed invalid rather than throwing.

Assert the pairing IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: an APPLIED receipt has `refusal: null` and a populated `applied[]`; a REFUSED receipt has a populated `refusal` and — this is the half that rots — does NOT claim migrations it did not apply. A receipt type that permits both members populated at once is how a REFUSED record later reads as a success.

NO COMMAND KIND AND NO ROSTER BACKFILL (rail 4). Verified at plan time: `internal.*` receipt kinds sit OUTSIDE PAYLOAD_KEYS, the registry and the MCP roster entirely (`grep -n "internal\." apps/daemon/src/daemon-command-vocabulary.ts` returns 0), exactly as `internal.repository.publish_receipt` does. So this receipt costs no vocabulary, registry, allowlist or contracts edit. If you find yourself opening daemon-command-vocabulary.ts, stop — `deployment.migrate_down` and its backfill belong to the sibling publish row.

RED TESTS FIRST for the ordering and the safety property — the two arms this row exists for. Both run OFFLINE through injectable docker/pg ports; only DoD 5's round trip needs a real database.

  1. ORDERING (DoD 1). With ports that RECORD their call order, assert `pg_dump` COMPLETED before the first migration ran. Assert on the recorded ORDER, not on both having happened — an arm that only checks both occurred stays green when they swap. DoD 1 explicitly requires the mutation too: step 6 makes the service migrate-then-backup and this arm must go RED. An ordering property that has never been seen red is not evidence.
  2. THE CENTRAL SAFETY PROPERTY (DoD 2). When the backup fails, ZERO migrations are applied — and the assertion READS THE SCHEMA, not the return value. A refusal that returned correctly while a migration already ran is precisely the scenario the receipt exists to make impossible, and a return-value assertion cannot tell those apart. Assert the schema is untouched, AND assert code `MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED` with its layer.
  3. MIGRATION_FAILED NAMES THE FILE (DoD 6). Assert code AND layer AND that the failing migration's filename appears in the detail. A generic failure is undiagnosable from a receipt and sends a seat to read every migration. On this path assert the receipt is REFUSED with the failing migration named AND the backup still recorded — the backup survives a failed migration, which is the whole point of taking it first.
  4. THE RECEIPT ROUND-TRIPS FROM A REAL STORE (DoD 3). Write it, read it back, assert every member including `backupRef`'s sha256 and that the file exists at the step-2 path.

Every arm asserts against the production surface; do not write a helper that re-derives ordering or refusal shape.

THE ENGINE — a new focused module plus its `.js` bridge, under apps/daemon/src/repository/ (say which directory and why in the step note).

SHAPE: injectable docker/pg/filesystem ports and a clock, so every arm in step 4 runs without a real database. Sequence, and the order is the row's reason for existing: take the `pg_dump` backup -> verify it completed and record its sha256 -> apply pending migrations -> write the receipt. A failure at the backup step returns MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED and applies NOTHING.

TEARDOWN IN A `finally`, NOT AFTER THE ASSERTIONS (DoD 7). Every disposable database, container, temp directory and child process is released on EVERY exit path INCLUDING the throwing one. Reuse child 2's lifecycle rather than writing a second one — a second independently-written cleanup is how one of them leaks, and child 2's row carries that same rail.

PROCESS INVOCATION, and this repo has been bitten here: invoke `pg_dump`, `psql` and `docker` as BARE EXECUTABLES with argv arrays under `shell:false`. Never a hard-coded `.cmd` (the measured Windows runtime returns EINVAL for hard-coded `.cmd` launchers — same class as the pnpm launcher rail), never a shell string (a shell re-parses arguments), never a chained command (a `;`-chain reports only the last command's status and a pipe reports the tail's). Preserve the exact exit status; if you must capture a pipeline's first stage, capture `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`.

Keep the module under 250 lines; split before 400. Do not grow `activation-receipts-measure.ts` — this row only exports two constants from it.

THE RESTORE ROUND TRIP — DoD 5, and the reason it is in THIS row rather than deferred: the row that writes the backup is the row that proves it can be read back. A backup nobody has restored is a file, not a safety net.

Against a REAL disposable PostgreSQL from child 2's lifecycle: create a known schema, back it up, CHANGE the schema, restore from the backup, and assert the schema matches the original. Assert the schema itself — the tables and columns — not merely that the restore command exited 0. A restore that silently restored nothing exits 0.

GATE IT THE WAY THE REPO ALREADY GATES REAL-DOCKER WORK, and copy the discipline exactly: `apps/daemon/src/repository/deployment/deployment-image-build.test.ts:183` uses `it.runIf(RUN_BUILD)`, and its docstring at :33 records that with the flag SET and no docker the arm FAILS LOUDLY with a `DEPLOY_DOCKER_UNAVAILABLE:` line rather than skipping. A gate that silently skips while its flag is on is how a whole leg quietly stops being tested — and for THIS row that would mean shipping an unproven restore, which is the exact thing DoD 5 exists to prevent.

Say in the completion record WHICH arms ran and which were gated out, with the flag and its value. An unqualified "suite green" here would hide that the restore was never actually performed.

Leave the host clean: an `afterEach` removes anything the arm created — container, temp directory, dump file — tolerating "already gone", so even a failing arm leaks nothing.

GATES, DRILLS, RECORD.

GATES, each STANDALONE and FOREGROUND — no pipe, no `;` chain, no `&&`:
  1. `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`
  2. `pnpm typecheck`
READ THE OUTPUT, NOT THE EXIT CODE: a missed `--filter` exits 0, and "No test files found" / "0 passed" are also exit 0. The discriminator is `Test Files N passed` with N nonzero — quote it for both. DoD 8 is explicit: root `pnpm test` covers NO `apps/**` file, so SAY that rather than quoting a bare root count line. Name `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` as the complete_task verification command.

The daemon suite is slow (~22 min) and flaky on this branch (two back-to-back baselines gave `17 failed | 416 passed` then `10 failed | 423 passed`, dominated by 30000ms timeouts), so attribute red by PATH per global rail 3, never by whole-suite delta. Run the touched suites targeted first.

DRILL 1, REQUIRED BY DoD 1 ITSELF. Mutate the service to migrate-then-backup. The ordering arm MUST go red. If it stays green the arm is checking that both happened rather than their order — strengthen it before accepting.
DRILL 2, THE SAFETY PROPERTY. Make the backup-failure path apply migrations anyway. The DoD-2 arm must go red ON THE SCHEMA ASSERTION, not only on a code check. If only the code assertion reds, the arm is reading the return value and would miss the case that actually loses data.
DRILL 3, THE RECEIPT PAIRING. Populate both `refusal` and the success members at once. The pairing arm must go red — otherwise a REFUSED receipt can later read as a success.

RESTORE PROOF, global rail 13. `git status --porcelain` the exact mutated paths BEFORE drilling. `activation-receipts-measure.ts` is TRACKED, so an empty `git diff -- <path>` is valid proof, run in a call SEPARATE from the restore. The NEW modules you created are UNTRACKED and `git diff` is BLIND to them — back each up out of tree (%TEMP%, suffixed with your worker id) before mutating and prove the restore by SHA256 equality against that backup.

COMPLETION RECORD states: whether the deploy row (task-5d309484) had landed and, if not, that this shipped behind its own entry point; how the backup path reuses activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33 (exported or derived) with the grep proving the resulting path; that no command kind, roster or contracts file was touched; which arms were docker-gated and the flag; and the three drill outcomes with their restore proofs.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
SPLITTING THIS ROW — considered because it carries EIGHT DoD items, one over the guidance ceiling. Rejected: this is already a SPIDR child of a parent that measured far over the cap, its rails fence out the command kind, the UI, Playwright, the live drive and the docs, and the remaining items are facets of ONE deliverable — the engine and the safety property that makes it safe. The natural cut lines all run through the backup/migrate ordering, and separating "write the backup" from "prove it restores" is exactly the split the row's own rail 2 forbids: the row that writes the backup is the row that proves it can be read back. Measured shape is 7 steps over ~8 files, inside both caps.

MINTING A NEW BACKUP LOCATION — rejected by rail 3 and by measurement: a second location is a second place to look during an incident, and the literals are already transcribed twice.

REFACTORING daemon-main-activation-boot.test.ts to import the exported constants — rejected as scope. It is a file this row does not own and tidying it would put an unrelated test in the diff; recorded as a follow-up observation instead.

ASSERTING DoD 2 ON THE RETURN VALUE — rejected explicitly in the plan. A refusal that returned correctly while a migration already ran is the exact data-losing scenario, and only a schema assertion distinguishes them. Drill 2 requires the SCHEMA assertion to be the one that reds.

WIRING INTO THE DEPLOY PATH — not assumed. task-5d309484 is a SIBLING feature row so no dependsOn is allowed (rail 6); the plan has the worker measure whether it landed and, if not, ship behind this row's own entry point and say so, rather than wiring into a path that does not exist or building a second one.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights:
MEASURED 2026-09-05 by architect-aa54e231 on branch moe/work-2026-09-04. The row's own description was measured by architect-fa3a3e17; I re-verified every claim it makes and all four hold.

THE GAP IS REAL IN EVERY DIRECTION: `git grep -c "migrate_down|MIGRATION_BACKUP_FAILED|moe-migration-receipt" -- apps packages` returns NOTHING. No migration surface exists, so nothing here duplicates a landed one.

AND `daemon-main-activation-boot.test.ts:35-36` ALREADY re-declares both literals locally, joining them at :156. So a third transcription is what this row must not add — which strengthens DoD 4's export-or-derive instruction beyond what the row's own description says. The plan also tells the worker NOT to tidy that test file: it is out of scope and would put an unrelated test in the diff.

THE RECEIPT SHAPE TO MIRROR, verified: `publish-receipt-contracts.ts` has `PUBLISH_RECEIPT_VERSION` (:16), `PublishRefusal { code, detail }` (:36-39), `PublishReceiptV1` (:41-53) carrying `outcome: "PUSHED" | "REFUSED"` beside `refusal: PublishRefusal | null` and nullable success members (`sha`, `branch`, `url`), and a typed decode union `PublishReceiptDecodeResult` (:55-57) so a malformed receipt answers invalid rather than throwing. The null-pairing — exactly one side populated — is what makes a REFUSED receipt unambiguous, and the plan requires it asserted in BOTH directions.

NO ROSTER BACKFILL, verified: `internal.*` receipt kinds sit outside PAYLOAD_KEYS, the registry and the MCP roster entirely (`grep -n "internal\." apps/daemon/src/daemon-command-vocabulary.ts` = 0), exactly as `internal.repository.publish_receipt` does. So `moe-migration-receipt/1` costs no vocabulary, registry, allowlist or contracts edit — which is what keeps this row inside the file cap.

THE REAL-DATABASE GATE PATTERN comes from the deployment lane: `deployment-image-build.test.ts:183` uses `it.runIf(RUN_BUILD)` and its docstring at :33 records that with the flag SET and no docker the arm FAILS LOUDLY rather than skipping. That is the shape DoD 5's restore arm should copy — a silently-skipping gate would ship an unproven restore, which is precisely what DoD 5 exists to prevent.
planningNotes.risks:
1. THE ORDERING ARM THAT ONLY CHECKS BOTH HAPPENED. It stays green when backup and migrate swap, which is the failure that loses data. DoD 1 itself demands the mutation drill; drill 1 makes it mandatory.

2. DoD 2 ASSERTED ON THE RETURN VALUE. A correct-looking refusal returned while a migration already ran is indistinguishable from a real refusal unless the arm reads the SCHEMA. Drill 2 requires the schema assertion to be the one that reds — if only the code assertion reds, the arm would miss the data-losing case entirely.

3. A SILENTLY-SKIPPING RESTORE GATE. DoD 5's whole point is that an unrestored backup is a file, not a safety net. A gate that skips while its flag is on ships exactly that, and an unqualified "suite green" hides it. The plan requires the loud-failure shape and requires the record to name which arms ran.

4. A RECEIPT THAT PERMITS BOTH MEMBERS POPULATED. Then a REFUSED record later reads as a success. Drill 3 exists for this; the pairing must be asserted in both directions, and the REFUSED direction is the one that rots because the natural test only checks the happy path.

5. A THIRD TRANSCRIPTION OF THE BACKUP PATH. Two already exist. A third drifts, and during an incident an operator looks in the wrong place.

6. A SECOND CONTAINER LIFECYCLE. Child 2 owns one and carries a rail saying a second independently-written cleanup is how one of them leaks. This row reuses it rather than standing up its own.

7. WINDOWS PROCESS INVOCATION. Hard-coded `.cmd` launchers return EINVAL on the measured runtime; a shell string re-parses arguments; a `;`-chain reports only the last status and a pipe reports the tail's. All three would make a backup or restore failure read as a success.

8. SCOPE LEAK INTO THE COMMAND KIND. `deployment.migrate_down` and its roster backfill belong to the sibling publish row, and the 13-file cost of publishing a kind on this board is documented. Opening daemon-command-vocabulary.ts is the signal to stop.
